q.t: How many lines can pass through two given points?
q.e: Once a straight line must go through both points its direction is fixed — any other path through both would have to bend.

q.t: How many lines can pass through one point?
q.e: With only one point to pass through, the line can point in any direction — like spokes spinning round a hub.

q.t: A ray has …
o: one starting point and goes on forever in one direction
no end points and goes both ways
q.e: A ray starts at one point and never stops in one direction, like a torch beam.

q.t: How many degrees make a right angle?
q.e: A right angle is a quarter turn: 360° ÷ 4 = 90°.

q.t: How many degrees make a straight angle?
q.e: A straight angle is half a turn: 360° ÷ 2 = 180°.

q.t: How many degrees make a full turn?
q.e: A full turn is divided into 360 equal parts called degrees.

q.t: An angle of 40° is …
q.e: Acute angles are less than 90°.

q.t: An angle of 130° is …
q.e: Obtuse angles are more than 90° but less than 180°.

q.t: In ∠PQR, which point is the vertex?
q.e: The vertex is always the middle letter of an angle's name.

q.t: The shortest path between two points is a …
q.e: Of all paths from A to B, the straight one — the line segment AB — is the shortest.

q.t: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 2 o'clock?
q.e: 12 equal gaps share 360°, so each gap is 30°. Two gaps: 60°.

q.t: What is the angle between the clock hands at 4 o'clock?
q.e: Four gaps of 30° each: 120°.

q.t: Is ray OA the same as ray AO?
o: No — they start at different points and go opposite ways
Yes — the letters are the same
Yes — rays can be read either way
q.e: A ray's first letter is its start. OA starts at O; AO starts at A.

q.t: B lies on ray OA, beyond O in A's direction. Can ray OA also be called ray OB?
o: No — B is a different point
No — rays need their end point
Only if B is after A
q.e: A ray is fixed by where it starts and which way it goes, not by which point names the direction.

q.t: An angle of 200° is …
q.e: Reflex angles are more than 180° but less than 360°.

q.t: If you make the arms of an angle twice as long, the angle …
q.e: An angle measures the turn between the arms, not how far they reach.

q.t: A protractor's arms read 20 and 75. What is the angle?
q.e: If neither arm is on 0, subtract: 75 − 20 = 55°.

q.t: Two lines that meet at a right angle are called …
q.e: Perpendicular lines meet at 90°.

q.t: A straight angle is how many right angles?
Points L, M, P, Q, R are joined in a chain L–M–P–Q–R. How many line segments are there?
q.e: LM, MP, PQ, QR. Five points in a chain give four segments.

q.t: A straight angle is split into 8 equal angles. How big is each?
The Ashoka Chakra has 24 equally spaced spokes. What is the angle between two neighbouring spokes?
q.e: 360° shared equally among 24 gaps: 360 ÷ 24 = 15°.

q.t: Between spokes of the Ashoka Chakra (multiples of 15°), what is the largest acute angle?
q.e: Multiples of 15°: 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90. 90° is a right angle, not acute, so the largest acute one is 75°.

q.t: The small angle at a vertex is 100°. What is the reflex angle on the other side?
q.e: The two angles together go once round the point: 360° − 100° = 260°.

q.t: B, E, R are on a straight line and ∠TER = 80°. What is ∠BET?
q.e: ∠BET and ∠TER together make the straight angle BER of 180°, so ∠BET = 180° − 80° = 100°.

q.t: You mark 3 points, no three on a line, and join every pair. How many lines do you get?
q.e: AB, BC, CA — one for each pair.

q.t: You mark 4 points, no three on a line, and join every pair. How many lines do you get?
q.e: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD — each of the 4 points pairs with 3 others, and each line is counted twice: 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6.

q.t: Why can't we always call an angle ∠P by its vertex alone?
o: Several angles may share vertex P, so ∠P wouldn't say which
P might not be a point
q.e: ∠P is fine only when exactly one angle has vertex P.

q.t: On a protractor, ∠POQ = 35° and ∠POR = 95° (same side). What is ∠QOR?
q.e: ∠QOR is the part of ∠POR left after ∠POQ: 95 − 35 = 60°.

q.t: What is the angle between the clock hands at 9 o'clock (the smaller angle)?
q.e: From 9 to 12 is 3 gaps of 30° = 90°. (Going the long way round would be 270°, the reflex angle.)

q.t: I am an acute angle (whole degrees). 4 times me is still acute, but 5 times me is obtuse. What is the SMALLEST I can be?
q.k: min(a for a in range(1,90) if 4*a<90 and 90<5*a<180)
q.e: 4 × me < 90 → me < 22.5. 5 × me > 90 → me > 18. Whole numbers: 19, 20, 21, 22. The smallest is 19 (18 fails: 5 × 18 = 90 is a right angle).

q.t: Same puzzle: what is the LARGEST the angle can be?
q.k: max(a for a in range(1,90) if 4*a<90 and 90<5*a<180)
q.e: Me < 22.5 because 4 × me must stay below 90. 22 works (88 acute, 110 obtuse); 23 gives 92, not acute.

q.t: With 4 points (no three on a line) and all 6 lines drawn, how many angles can you name using only the 4 points?
q.e: At each point three lines meet, making 3 angles (e.g. ∠BAC, ∠CAD, ∠BAD). 4 points × 3 = 12.

q.t: A letter Y has three angles around its centre: 150°, 60° and one more. What is the third?
q.e: Angles all the way round a point make a full turn: 360 − 150 − 60 = 150°.

q.t: What is the reflex angle between the clock hands at 4 o'clock?
q.e: The small angle is 4 × 30° = 120°; the reflex angle is the rest of the turn: 360 − 120 = 240°.

q.t: Why is folding a straight crease exactly onto itself guaranteed to make a right angle?
o: The two halves coincide, so the two angles are equal halves of 180°
q.e: Superimposition shows the two angles are equal; two equal angles making a straight angle are 90° each.

q.t: Why is 360 a convenient number of degrees for a full turn?
o: It divides exactly by every number from 1 to 10 except 7
It is the number of days in every year
q.e: 360 splits evenly into halves, thirds, quarters, fifths, sixths, eighths, ninths and tenths — whole-number degrees for many equal parts.

q.t: Two perpendicular creases cross at a point. How many right angles are there around that point?
q.e: The full turn of 360° is cut into equal right angles: 360 ÷ 90 = 4.

q.t: A full turn is split into 5 equal angles. How big is each?
∠AOB = ∠AOX + ∠XOY + ∠YOB. Which is larger, ∠AOB or ∠XOY?
o: ∠AOB, because ∠XOY is only one part of it
q.e: A whole angle is larger than any of the pieces it is made from.
